SEC17A-01.explanation: In a "not X but Y" subject, the verb agrees with the affirmed member, Y. Here the sentence denies "the ears" and affirms "each outgoing call's rapid pitch sweep," whose head noun "sweep" is singular, so the verb must be singular even though "ears" is plural. The sweep is also the thing doing the acting: it directs "the bat's path around an obstacle," which is the verb's object, delayed past the interrupting phrase "during the final milliseconds of an approach." So the verb must be active: "was steering." "were steering" is active but plural, agreeing with the denied "ears" rather than with "sweep." "was steered" is singular but passive; it would say the sweep was guided by something else and would leave "the bat's path" with no grammatical role. "were steered" is both plural and passive.

SEC17A-02.explanation: When each part of a compound subject is introduced by "every," the subject is treated as singular: "every pastor and every schoolteacher" takes a singular verb, even though the two nouns are joined by "and." The sentence opens with "Since the first freeze date ... was written into a parish ledger" and continues "so the ledger now gives," so the recording is an activity running from a past starting point up to the present, which requires a perfect form: "has been recording." "have been recording" has the right aspect but is plural, treating the "and" as if it formed a plural subject. "is recording" is singular but present progressive, which describes only what is happening now and does not express a span running from the "Since" starting point up to the present. "were recording" is plural and past progressive, which places the activity at some past moment rather than across that span.

SEC17A-03.explanation: The subject of the main clause is "such a lens," which is singular; the plural nouns "prisms," "workshops," "tiers," and "frames" all sit inside the fronted participial phrase and cannot be the subject. The lens is also not the thing doing the moving: it is carried somewhere "in numbered sections" because no crate or hold can take it whole, so the verb must be passive. The passage is in the present tense ("can stand," "goes up," "can accommodate"), so the key is "is transported." "are transported" is passive but plural, agreeing with the plural nouns of the opening phrase. "transports" is singular and present but active; a lens does not transport anything, and the verb would have no object. "is transporting" is singular but also active, and it likewise makes the lens the mover, with nothing for it to move.

SEC17A-04.explanation: The relative pronoun "that" refers to the whole compound "the skull and the lower jaw": the clause says the two bones were "still in their original position relative to each other," and "each other" can only refer to two things. So the verb must be plural, even though "jaw," the noun right before "that," is singular. The verb also has to describe the bones as they were when the excavators "first exposed" them; the next sentence says both bones "have since been lifted out," so they no longer lie there, and a form reaching up to the present is impossible. The key is the plural past progressive "were lying." "was lying" has the right tense but is singular, agreeing with "jaw" alone. "are lying" is plural, but the present progressive says the bones lie in place now, which the second sentence contradicts. "has lain" is singular, and its present perfect likewise reaches up to the present, wrong on both counts.

SEC17A-05.explanation: In a sentence that begins "So + adjective," the verb comes before its subject. The subject here is "the hall's early reverberation measurements across different seating sections," whose head noun "measurements" is plural, so the verb must be plural. The tense is set by the end of the sentence: the panels "have since brought the readings into a narrow and consistent range," so the unevenness belongs to the past and no longer holds. The key is therefore "uneven were." "uneven was" is past but singular, as though "hall's" or "sound" were the subject. "uneven are" is plural but present, which would say the readings are still uneven despite the panels having since evened them out. "uneven has been" is singular, and its present perfect reaches up to the present, so it is wrong in number and, like "uneven are," contradicts the panels' later correction.

SEC17A-06.explanation: In a comparative clause of the form "as + auxiliary + subject," the auxiliary stands in for the verb of the first clause and must match its type. The first clause's verbs, "hold back" and "release," are ordinary lexical verbs in the simple present, so the stand-in is a form of "do." The postposed subject is "the pale, slender, sweetly scented trumpets," whose head noun "trumpets" is plural, so the auxiliary must be plural: "as do." "as does" is the right auxiliary type but singular. "as are" agrees with "trumpets" but substitutes "be" for a lexical verb, producing "release ... as are the trumpets," which does not complete the comparison. "as is" is the wrong auxiliary type and singular.

SEC17A-07.explanation: The sentence is inverted: the fronted phrase "Far more puzzling to the specialists" is a complement, and the subject follows the verb. That subject is "the abrupt and nearly simultaneous collapse of elm pollen," whose head noun "collapse" is singular, so the verb must be singular even though "specialists," the noun right before the blank, is plural. The aspect is set by the appositive at the end: the collapse is "a problem that has divided them from the earliest coring surveys to the present day," so the puzzle continues up to now, which requires the present perfect "has been." "have been" has the right aspect but is plural, agreeing with "specialists." "was once" is singular but says the collapse used to be puzzling and no longer is, contradicting a problem that still divides researchers "to the present day." "were once" is plural and wrong in the same way.

SEC17A-08.explanation: The verb belongs to the clause reporting what the astronomer "found" in the past, and the action it names happened even earlier: the compiler did his work before he "died," and he died "decades before the problem came to light." An action completed before another past event is expressed with the past perfect, so the key is "had transposed." "has transposed" is present perfect, which connects the action to the present and does not fit a report framed by "found" and "came to light," about a man long dead. "was transposing" is past progressive, which would place the compiler in the middle of transposing digits at the time of the discovery, when he had died decades earlier. "transposes" is simple present and breaks the past frame entirely.

SEC17A-09.explanation: The sentence opens with a long subordinate clause, "Although the wave models of the time predicted that such giants should form perhaps once in ten thousand years at any given spot," and the main clause is "a laser gauge on a North Sea gas platform recorded one." An introductory subordinate clause is joined to the main clause with a comma, so the key is "spot, a." "spot; a" uses a semicolon, which may only join independent clauses; the "Although" clause cannot stand alone, so it would be left as a fragment. "spot: a" uses a colon, which must follow a complete independent clause; what precedes it here is only the subordinate "Although" clause. "spot a" omits any mark, running the long introductory clause straight into the main clause's subject, so that "spot a laser gauge" reads as one phrase.

SEC17A-10.explanation: Two independent clauses meet at the blank: "The compound was present only in minute amounts and broke down whenever it was heated" and "a team that processed several tons of bran eventually obtained a few grams of pure crystals." The contrast that "however" signals is between them: the difficulties of the first clause against the success of the second. So "however" belongs to the second clause, and a semicolon must separate the clauses before it: "heated; however, a." "heated, however; a" attaches "however" to the first clause, where it would contrast the compound's fragility with the previous sentence; but that sentence also describes frustration, so there is no contrast there, and the real turn to success is left unmarked. "heated: however, a" uses a colon, which introduces an explanation or elaboration of the preceding clause, not a contrast with it. "heated, however, a" joins two independent clauses with only commas, a comma splice.

SEC17B-01.explanation: Because of "the only," the relative pronoun "that" refers to "one" (the moth), not to "visitors": the moth is the single member of the group that does this, so the verb in the relative clause must be singular. The moth is also the one doing the carrying, and the thing carried, "pollen," appears later in the sentence as the verb's object, so the verb must be active: "is carrying." "are carrying" is active but plural, agreeing with "visitors" as if the clause described the whole group rather than the only one of them. "is carried" is singular but passive, which would make the moth the thing carried and leave "pollen" with no grammatical role. "are carried" is both plural and passive.

SEC17B-02.explanation: In a cleft sentence such as "it is the juvenile shells ... that," the verb in the "that" clause agrees with the noun that has been singled out, "the juvenile shells," not with the singular "it is" that introduces it, so the verb must be plural. The shells are also what the curators and earlier cataloguers get wrong; they do not identify anything themselves, and the clause names nothing that they would be misidentifying, so the verb must be passive: "are misidentified." "is misidentified" is passive but singular, agreeing with "it is" instead of with "shells." "are misidentifying" is plural but active, which would make the shells the ones doing the identifying and leaves the verb without the object it requires. "misidentifies" is both singular and active.

SEC17B-03.explanation: The verb belongs to the clause introduced by "that," whose subject is "photoperiod" (day length), a singular noun; the long plural subject of the main clause, "The botanists and climatologists ... ," goes with "argue," not with this verb. Photoperiod is also what does the determining, and what it determines, "the week in which beech buds finally open," follows the interrupting phrase as the verb's object, so the verb must be active, and the present perfect fits a pattern holding "across those decades" of records: "has determined." "have determined" is active but plural, agreeing with "botanists and climatologists." "is determined" is singular but passive, which would make photoperiod the thing determined and leave "the week" with no grammatical role. "are determined" is both plural and passive.

SEC17B-04.explanation: A subject of the form "more than one" plus a singular noun ("more than one core") takes a singular verb, even though it refers to several cores. The time frame is set by "Until the field team switched to chilled drill bits": the damage happened during a past period that ended with the switch, and the bits "now keep the mud frozen," so the problem no longer occurs. That calls for the simple past: "was in pieces." "is in pieces" is singular but present, describing a current state that the switch has ended. "has been in pieces" is singular but present perfect, which would stretch the damage up to the present, contradicting the past cutoff set by "until ... switched." "have been in pieces" has the same tense problem and is also plural, treating "more than one core" as plural.

SEC17B-05.explanation: After a fronted "Not until ..." phrase, the sentence inverts, and with a base-form main verb ("hatch") the inversion uses a form of "do" that agrees with the subject. That subject comes after the blank: its head is "eggs" ("the tiny, thick-walled, and nearly indestructible resting eggs"), which is plural. The passage describes a recurring natural cycle in the present tense ("spend," "hold," "refill"), so the auxiliary must be present and plural: "do the." "does the" is present but singular, as if the subject were singular. "did the" is past, which does not fit a cycle described in the present tense. "is the" cannot combine with the base form "hatch" at all; "is" would need a participle ("is ... hatching"), and it is also singular.

SEC17B-06.explanation: This sentence is inverted: it opens with "Bundled with the envelopes," and its subject follows the verb. The subject is "the farmer's own handwritten account," whose head "account" is singular, so the verb must be singular even though the plural "envelopes" comes just before the blank. The tense is set by what happened afterward: "the library has since transferred it to the county archive," so the account is no longer bundled with the envelopes, and the sentence must describe how the box was when it was donated ("The box held"). That calls for the past: "was evidently." "is evidently" is singular but present, claiming the account is still in the box, which the transfer rules out. "has evidently been" is singular but present perfect, which would extend the bundling up to the present, also ruled out by the transfer. "were evidently" is past but plural, agreeing with "envelopes."

SEC17B-07.explanation: In "Such ... that" sentences the verb comes before its subject. The subject here is "the steady, year-round browsing pressure," whose head "pressure" is singular; the plural nouns that follow ("goat herds," "farmers," "animals") belong to modifying phrases. The time frame is set by "ever since farmers stopped penning their animals," which describes a situation running from a past starting point up to the present, where seedlings "now" fail to survive; that requires the present perfect. So the answer is "has been." "have been" has the right tense but is plural, agreeing with "goat herds" instead of "pressure." "had been" is past perfect, which needs a later past moment to look back from, but the result is stated in the present ("now survives"). "is now" is present but cannot carry a span that began "ever since" a past event.

SEC17B-08.explanation: The verb completes the clause reported by "The restoration trust has announced that ... ," a present-perfect reporting verb, so the prediction is made from the present looking forward. It is also tied to the time clause "once the chamber is refilled and boats return," whose present-tense verbs refer to future events; such a clause pairs with "will" in the main clause. So the answer is "will remain watertight." "would remain watertight" is tempting because the nearby verbs "shaped," "were air-dried," and "cut" are past, but those describe how the gates were made, not when the trust speaks; "would" belongs with a past reporting verb or past-tense time clause ("once the chamber was refilled"), not with "has announced" and "is refilled." "remained watertight" is simple past, describing something already over. "had remained watertight" is past perfect, which needs a later past moment that the sentence never supplies.

SEC17B-09.explanation: The subject of the first clause is "The deep blue pigment the illuminators of a single workshop ground by hand from imported lapis lazuli": the noun "pigment" is modified by a restrictive relative clause ("[that] the illuminators ... ground ... from imported lapis lazuli") whose relative pronoun has been left out. The verb of the main clause is "cost," and no punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, so the answer is "lazuli cost." "lazuli, cost" puts a single comma between the subject and the verb; a restrictive relative clause is not set off by commas, so there is no pair for this comma to close. "lazuli: cost" is wrong because a colon must follow a complete independent clause, and everything before it is only the subject, a noun phrase with no main verb of its own ("ground" belongs to the relative clause). "lazuli—cost" is wrong because a single dash would mark a break after a complete clause or close a dash pair, and here there is neither: no clause is complete before it and no earlier dash opens an interruption, so it simply cuts the subject off from its verb.

SEC17B-10.explanation: Everything before the blank, "their account books show that they feared one thing more than shipwreck or a collapse in prices," is a complete clause that announces "one thing" without naming it. What follows, "a single heavy rain in the final weeks before the harvest," is a noun phrase that identifies that thing. A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation after a complete clause, so the answer is "prices: a." "prices; a" is wrong because a semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and "a single heavy rain ..." has no verb. "prices, a" makes the noun phrase read as another item tacked onto "shipwreck or a collapse in prices," as if rain were a third thing they feared less than the "one thing," which breaks the sentence's logic. "prices a" runs the noun phrase directly into "collapse in prices" with no mark at all, leaving it with no grammatical connection to the sentence.
